entry.title: Anthropic’s IPO Marketing Meets Extinction Risk
entry.content:
Are we sleepwalking our way into AI-caused extinction? It feels a little like that, given an Anthropic researcher’s X post on Tuesday night that there’s a greater than 10% chance that “AI could kill all humans” within the next decade! Despite that rather gruesome note, for tech executives posting on X today, it was business as usual. (See our detailed report on the episode here).

Plenty of dark humor circulated about the researcher’s post, however—this one joking about a Wall Street analyst asking Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the “extinction number” on an earnings call is possibly the best. That joke also highlighted the reality that Anthropic will shortly be marketing its IPO. How will its executives handle the warning on the Wall Street investor road show?

entry.title: Why An Anthropic Researcher’s Terminator-Style Warning Caught Fire
entry.content:
An Anthropic safety researcher’s warning Tuesday that his company believes AI “could kill all humans” within a decade has reverberated throughout Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Washington, potentially complicating the Claude maker’s upcoming initial public offering and its efforts to repair ties with U.S. political leaders.

As the comment circulated around the internet and on TV broadcasts, some Anthropic employees and other AI staffers defended their efforts to minimize harm their technology might cause—while acknowledging there was much work to do. Paul Christiano, whom OpenAI just tapped as a board director of a nonprofit that oversees the company, echoed the Anthropic warning in a statement Wednesday, saying that “If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment”—or safety constraints—“I expect we will permanently lose control of it. If that happens then most people could die.”

entry.title: OpenAI Restricts Adobe and Other Competitors From Advertising in ChatGPT
entry.content:
OpenAI has told some business partners that it will no longer accept advertising in ChatGPT for image- and audio-generating products—which compete with its own features.

The change, which hasn’t been previously reported or reflected in its published ads policy, blindsided existing advertisers such as Adobe, which sells such products. And if extended to other competing products, the new policy could narrow OpenAI’s potential ad revenue. OpenAI has given investors aggressive projections for ad growth, which it sees as a key way to make money off its large audience of people who don’t pay for the service.

entry.title: OpenAI Math Result Stokes Data-Sharing Concerns
entry.content:
In case you missed it: we got an eye-catching X post on Tuesday night from Evan Hubinger, a leader of Anthropic's alignment efforts. Responding to the resignation announcement of an Anthropic employee who warned that AI companies aren’t doing enough to ensure AI won't kill humanity, Hubinger wrote that the employee is “correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.” Hubinger added that he was worried about future AI models, not those currently available, but still, yikes!

Meanwhile, our colleague Jyoti sizes up the significance of Meta’s new personal AI agent, Muse, unveiled on Tuesday. That’s below. But before we get to that:

This may go down as the year the AI industry got a crash course in mathematics. Breakthroughs in AI models have yielded announcements on such arcane subjects as the “Erdős unit distance problem” and the “Jacobian Conjecture,” which observers have watched as an indicator of AI progress in other domains.

The latest announcement, OpenAI's claim on Tuesday that it had solved the vexing “Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem,” has drawn attention for another reason: questions over whether its math-genius models may have gained an edge by incorporating data from two human mathematicians that had used OpenAI's Codex in their work on the same problem. Those questions fed into concerns about the possibility of AI companies learning from customers’ use of their AI models to develop competing products.

entry.title: Confusion Reigns Over White House’s AI Whitelist
entry.content:
It may be one of the hottest tickets in corporate America right now: membership in the “trusted partner” program that allows companies to get access to the most advanced AI models before they’re released to the public. There’s just one problem: no one outside of the Trump administration has a clear idea how to get on that list.

As laid out in the administration’s executive order in early June, which established a voluntary testing framework for frontier AI models, these “trusted partners”— including banks, cybersecurity firms and power utilities—would use their access to sniff out potential vulnerabilities in their computer systems exposed by the new AI models.

entry.title: China Curbs Humanoid IPOs After Unitree’s Volatile Debut
entry.content:
Chinese regulators are tightening the approval for humanoid startups seeking to go public after a volatile debut by industry leader Unitree Robotics, as they aim to cool down a sizzling sector rife with copycats but little real technological breakthroughs.

The Chinese Securities Regulatory Commission recently gave its informal “window guidance” to some investment banks and investment firms that it is raising the bar for granting approval of humanoid IPOs, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Companies must demonstrate they can generate recurring revenue, are on a path to narrow their losses or achieve real innovation before approvals can be considered, the people added.

entry.title: Gimlet's Three-Tranche Deal Reveals AI Funding Frenzy
entry.content:
Gimlet Labs said late last week it had raised $300 million at a valuation of about $3 billion, in a round led by new investor Andreessen Horowitz. Today we have unreported details on how that round, which boosted its valuation by a whopping 16 times from its last PitchBook valuation, came together.

The three-year-old startup, which helps AI developers run models using different AI chips simultaneously, raised the round after the company’s executives told some potential investors that based on signed contracts, OpenAI was likely to spend more than $100 million a year on its services, according to a person familiar with the company. Such outlays, if they transpire, would be significant given it just emerged from stealth in October. 

This windfall would be in the future, however. “We have explored possibilities with Gimlet but we are not a paying customer,” said an OpenAI spokesperson.

entry.title: Why Price Cuts May Rattle Anthropic's IPO Pitch
entry.content:
Anthropic’s IPO paperwork is expected to become public sometime soon. But it was OpenAI finance chief Sarah Friar who drew a standing-room-only crowd Tuesday at San Francisco’s Palace Hotel, as Goldman Sachs kicked off its annual Communacopia + Technology conference with a Q&A with Friar. In her talk, Friar made clear how important price has become for determining model popularity—a potential problem for Anthropic, widely seen as the high-end AI provider.

Friar described how a price cut on OpenAI’s GPT 5.6 Luna model led to a tenfold increase in use, my colleague Anita Ramaswamy reported, giving OpenAI the highest market share on OpenRouter, a service developers use to access different models. We wrote in mid-August that Luna had generated more than twice the token usage of Anthropic’s Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 models on OpenRouter. Judging from Friar’s comments Tuesday, the increase in usage was enough to offset the price cut.
